title: Mishpatim: we will do, and we will hear (Exodus 24:7)
hook: the people promise to act before they fully understand

segments.voice: Yesterday, in Mishpatim, the widow and the orphan, and the promise that their cry is heard. Your line was God hears them. Whom did you stand beside? Today, the last day of the portion, and the people's answer. Day three hundred fifty-two.

Nobody learns to swim by reading about it. You can study the strokes, watch the videos, memorize how to breathe on every third stroke. None of it makes sense until you're in the water, swallowing some of the pool, and suddenly your body understands what the book was saying. Some things only make sense from the inside. Moses has written down the laws of the covenant. He reads them aloud to the whole people at the foot of the mountain. And they answer with two Hebrew words, in an order the rabbis would later dwell on.
screen: `NOBODY LEARNS TO SWIM BY READING.` → `SOME THINGS MAKE SENSE INSIDE.` → `THE PEOPLE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Here's their answer, in the old Jewish translation: "All that the LORD hath spoken will we do, and obey." In Hebrew the last words are na'aseh v'nishma. Na'aseh: we will do. V'nishma: and we will hear. The translation says obey, and that's one meaning of the word. But nishma also means hear, listen, understand. The same root as the Shema: hear, O Israel. So the people say: we will do, and then we will understand. Do first. Understanding second. The Talmud tells a story about it. When Israel put we will do before we will hear, it says, six hundred thousand angels came down and tied two crowns on each person, one for doing and one for hearing. A heavenly voice asked: who revealed to my children the secret the angels use? Because angels, a psalm says, do God's word first, and hear afterward. The Talmud also records a skeptic mocking a rabbi: you impetuous people, putting your mouths before your ears! The rabbi answered that people who walk in trust can afford to. Reasonable people can disagree about this, and Jewish tradition prizes asking questions too. The order isn't don't think. It's that some kinds of knowing only come by doing. Light the candles before you understand Shabbat. Sit with the mourners before you understand grief. And with that, Mishpatim ends: the details, the stranger, the enemy's donkey, the widow and orphan, and a people who said, we'll do it, and we'll learn.
screen: `ALL THAT THE LORD HATH SPOKEN.` · `NA'ASEH V'NISHMA: DO, THEN HEAR.` · `TWO CROWNS FROM THE ANGELS.` · `SOME KNOWING COMES BY DOING.` · then, large: `DO, THEN UNDERSTAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one thing to try first. Settle, and breathe. Think of a practice you've been curious about but keep putting off until you understand it better. Lighting candles on Friday night. A blessing before eating. A morning gratitude. A weekly walk in silence. Pick one. Don't argue with it yet. Just decide to try it once, this week, and let the understanding come later, if it comes. Picture yourself doing it. The bell holds the time.
Na'aseh v'nishma. We will do, and we will hear. The people's answer at Sinai, putting the doing before the understanding.
Your line: do, then understand. Today, try one practice before you understand it, and notice what it teaches you from the inside. Day three hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Na'aseh v'nishma is a phrase Jewish teachers return to when speaking about commitment, often cited to encourage people to begin a practice, like lighting Shabbat candles or saying a blessing, and let understanding grow from doing it.
